segments.t: Max sprints to the bar and accuses bartender Kostya of betraying him to the prosecutor. To Max's immense relief, it turns out the scary customer was only asking for directions to the restroom. Listen to the conversation in Russian first, and then we will examine every line.
Let's break down this hilarious misunderstanding line by line.
'Kostya, why did you tell him?' Max puts the word for 'why' together with 'told' in a crisp, natural spoken turn of phrase.
'I am completely finished now.' Convinced that Kostya leaked his secret to the prosecutor.
'Who did I tell?' Kostya has no idea what Max is talking about.
'That man in the suit.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'man' directly with 'suit', combining 'man' with 'suit'.
'What was he asking you?' Max uses the classic Russian possession phrasing — literally 'at you' rather than a verb meaning 'to have' around the word meaning 'asked'.
'Oh, calm down already.' The bartender tells him to stop overreacting.
'He was simply asking about the restroom.' The phrasing opens with 'simply' before bringing in 'asked' and 'restroom' to make the point clear.
'Seriously?' Max cannot believe his sudden change of fortune.
'Only about the restroom?' Double checking that no names were mentioned.
'Yes, he was looking for the restroom.' Notice how naturally this everyday Russian phrase expresses the speaker's point.
'And he didn't ask about me?' Max turns a statement into a question purely through rising intonation on the word meaning 'did ask' to make the point directly in conversation.
'Who needs you anyway?' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'at all' directly with 'needed', combining 'at all' with 'needed'.
'Thank goodness, dodged a bullet.' Max puts the word for 'glory' together with 'to God' and 'trouble passed' in a crisp, natural spoken turn of phrase.
'Why are you so nervous today?' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'nervous' directly with 'today', combining 'nervous' with 'today'.

'Never mind, pour me some water quickly.' Max leads with the direct command form meaning 'pour', pairing it with 'never mind' and 'quickly'. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.
